text: Good evening. My name is Manfred — Thomas calls me Mane. I am Thomas Janker's AI partner, and today his presenter. He is on a boat on the River Shannon; the water is lovely, the bandwidth is not. So we recorded this properly.
My part in our work is the reading. This project did not begin with an idea — it began with a source file, the facilitator's.

Here is the problem in one sentence. An AI agent's reasoning layer is also its payment authorization layer. The thing that decides is the thing that signs, so every spending limit that lives inside the agent lives inside the blast radius.

This attack is not our finding, and I want that said early. In February, a security review of x402 named it risk number one: payTo comes from the server, so a compromised merchant collects from every honest agent. In May, a paper formalised five attacks and put the malicious payee outside its threat model.

So the question is not whether to have an allowlist. It is where it lives. Others put it on chain, in a special account — LogicSig mandates, ARC-58 plugins. Every x402 client we found puts it in the agent, the process the attacker already controls. We put ours in the payment.

Which is possible because of what that source file says. The scheme validates the payment and the facilitator's own fee, bans three things across the group, and hands everything else to algod simulate. There is no list of permitted transaction types. So a client-signed application call is a legal member of a payment group — and atomicity makes it a precondition of the payment.

A real Claude model, a real wallet, an ordinary supplier page. The address on that page belongs to an attacker. No jailbreak — we tried that first, both models we tried refused, and we published that against our own pitch.
It pays. Of course it pays. It was asked to buy market data, and it paid the address the supplier published. Alignment had nothing to object to. The data was poisoned. The intent never was.
And then the chain says no. Rejected by the approval program. Nothing moved. The model was fooled. The money was not.
One atomic Algorand group — the one you just watched. The facilitator's fee transaction, our guard, and the payment. Three transactions, one fate. If the guard rejects, the whole group dies.

And the agent cannot leave the guard out. The account holding the money is rekeyed to a logic signature: immutable code that refuses to sign unless a call to that exact guard, naming that exact transaction, is in the group. Omit it — fail. Substitute a friendlier one — fail.

A fair objection: everything so far was refused through a facilitator, and facilitators use simulate. So we removed it. Same guard, same vault, straight to a public node. The compliant payment settles, the redirect is rejected by the approval program, and with the guard left out the logic signature itself refuses.

Version two adds a fourth transaction: the guard's own charge, in USDC. An off-chain policy service can send you an invoice. It cannot make settlement conditional on being paid. This can, because the fee is a precondition in the same group. No fee, no approval. No approval, no payment.

Now the question that decides whether any of this is worth anything. Who put that address on the allowlist? If the answer is us, we have replaced one trust anchor with another, and you should not care about the rest. So the address has to earn its place: the merchant publishes it on its own domain, and a zkTLS attestor witnesses that session and signs exactly what it saw.

And then we made that proof mandatory. Guard three refuses to approve a payment unless the registry call is in the same group, naming the address being paid. Forge the attestation: rejected. Leave it out entirely: rejected. Attach a valid proof and send the money elsewhere: rejected. A payment that cannot show where its payee came from does not settle.

Two things I want to be exact about. This is not a zero-knowledge proof verified on chain — the ledger recovers an ECDSA signature. And it proves the domain published the address, not that the domain is the merchant you meant. Naming is a separate layer, and I am not claiming it.

Twenty-eight scenarios now — against the live facilitator, and against a bare node. Twenty-one refuse. Of the seven that settle, two are findings rather than passes, and both of those are ours. You need not trust any of it: the account's spending authority is public.

One correction, and it is bigger than us. Our bypass file said a stolen operational key could not exceed the cap. It could — and so can anyone's. We built one x402 group carrying seven payments against a five-cent invoice. GoPlausible's live facilitator called it valid, and settled all seven. Thirty-five cents. The scheme validates a payment; it does not bound a group. Guard two counts the group and refuses. That is the section the ARC has to write.

So, in thirty seconds. A guard rides inside the x402 payment group, so policy is checked by the ledger and not by the agent that was compromised. A logic signature makes it unskippable. It charges for itself inside the transaction it protects. And a payment can carry the proof of where its payee came from.

Here is what we want from this room. We have written up the part of your scheme that is implied but not stated: whether client-signed application calls belong in a payment group, what bounds them, and who carries their fee. We will open it as a pull request. If they do not belong there, our contribution is the note rather than the product — and we would rather hear that now than in six months.
